teacher.title: Teacher
teacher.step.release: The object is released from rest. Initial velocity is zero at height h₀.
teacher.step.gravity_only: Only gravity acts on the object. Air resistance is ignored — ideal free fall.
teacher.step.accelerating: The object accelerates uniformly. Velocity increases linearly, displacement quadratically.
teacher.step.midpoint: Midpoint of the fall. Velocity is about 9.8 m/s. Notice the speed keeps increasing.
teacher.step.approaching_ground: Approaching the ground! Velocity nears maximum. Potential energy almost fully converted to kinetic.
teacher.step.impact: The object hits the ground. Velocity reverses direction on impact. Some energy is lost in the collision.
teacher.step.bounce: The object bounces back at 60% of impact speed. Energy is conserved but partially converted to other forms.
teacher.step.second_peak: The object reaches a new peak height, lower than the initial. It will fall again — this is real-world bouncing physics.
ui.drop_hint: Drag or click to upload problem
teacher.step1.title: Observe
teacher.step1.desc: The ball is released from rest at height h₀. Watch its motion: starting from zero, it gets faster and faster. This is the hallmark of free fall.
teacher.step2.title: Analyze Forces
teacher.step2.desc: Only gravity acts on the ball. Gravity points straight down with constant magnitude G = mg. Air resistance is ignored — ideal free fall.
teacher.step3.title: Build Model
teacher.step3.desc: Free fall is constant-acceleration motion. With a = g constant, we can use kinematic equations to describe position and velocity over time.
teacher.step4.title: Derive Formulas
teacher.step4.desc: Starting from v = v₀ + at, substitute v₀ = 0, a = g: v = gt. From s = v₀t + ½at²: h = h₀ − ½gt².
teacher.step5.title: Compute
teacher.step5.desc: Plug in h₀ = 10m, g = 9.8m/s². At impact h = 0: v = √(2 × 9.8 × 10) = √196 ≈ 14 m/s. Impact time t = √(2h₀/g) ≈ 1.43s.
teacher.step6.title: Verify
teacher.step6.desc: Watch the experiment to confirm: the ball indeed hits the ground at ~1.43s with velocity ~14 m/s. Theory matches experiment.
teacher.step7.title: Summary
teacher.step7.desc: Free fall is constant-acceleration motion under gravity alone. Key formulas: v = gt, h = ½gt², v² = 2gh. Understanding these is the foundation for more complex motion.
overlay.step.content.release: Ball released from rest. Initial velocity zero at height h₀.
overlay.step.content.gravity: Only gravity acts. Constant acceleration: g = 9.8 m/s² downward.
overlay.step.content.accelerating: Velocity increases linearly. At 0.6s: v = 5.88 m/s.
overlay.step.content.midpoint: At t = 1.0s, ball has fallen 4.9m, velocity is 9.8 m/s.
overlay.step.content.impact: Ball hits ground. Impact velocity ~14 m/s.
overlay.step.content.rebound: Ball bounces at 60% of impact speed. Energy partially lost.
overlay.step.content.second_fall: Ball reaches lower peak height, falls again.
plugin.projectile-motion.name: Projectile Motion
teacher.projectile.step1.title: Observe Motion
teacher.projectile.step1.desc: A ball is launched at an angle. Notice its trajectory is a parabola.
teacher.projectile.step2.title: Decompose Velocity
teacher.projectile.step2.desc: Split initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components. Horizontal stays constant, vertical is affected by gravity.
teacher.projectile.step3.title: Horizontal Motion
teacher.projectile.step3.desc: No horizontal force means constant horizontal velocity.
teacher.projectile.step4.title: Vertical Motion
teacher.projectile.step4.desc: Gravity causes constant downward acceleration. At the peak, vertical velocity is zero.
teacher.projectile.step4.formula: y(t) = v0 * sin(theta) * t - 1/2 * g * t^2
teacher.projectile.step5.title: Key Parameters
teacher.projectile.step5.desc: Range, max height, and flight time are all determined by initial speed and angle. Max range at 45 degrees.
teacher.projectile.step6.title: Impact Analysis
teacher.projectile.step6.desc: The ball hits the ground. Horizontal velocity persists, vertical velocity is downward.
teacher.projectile.step7.title: Knowledge Summary
teacher.projectile.step7.desc: Projectile motion is the superposition of constant horizontal velocity and free-fall vertical motion. The two dimensions are independent.
quiz.title: Check Understanding
quiz.freefall.q1: What force acts on an object in free fall?
quiz.freefall.q1.exp: In ideal free fall (ignoring air resistance), the object is only affected by gravity.
quiz.freefall.q2: What is the relationship between velocity v and time t in free fall?
quiz.freefall.q2.exp: Free fall is uniformly accelerated motion. v = g ? t, velocity is proportional to time.
plugin.inclined-plane.name: Inclined Plane
teacher.incline.step1.title: Observe Setup
teacher.incline.step1.desc: A block rests on an inclined plane. Gravity decomposes into components along and perpendicular to the incline.
teacher.incline.step2.title: Decompose Gravity
teacher.incline.step2.desc: The parallel component is mg*sin(theta). The perpendicular component is mg*cos(theta).
teacher.incline.step3.title: Force Analysis
teacher.incline.step3.desc: The incline provides normal force N = mg*cos(theta). With friction, f = mu*N, directed up the incline.
teacher.incline.step4.title: Newton 2nd Law
teacher.incline.step4.desc: Along the incline: mg*sin(theta) - mu*mg*cos(theta) = ma. If the net force is positive, the block accelerates.
teacher.incline.step5.title: Critical Angle
teacher.incline.step5.desc: When mu > tan(theta), friction is sufficient to hold the block at rest. This is called self-locking.
teacher.incline.step6.title: Reaching Bottom
teacher.incline.step6.desc: The block reaches the bottom of the incline with maximum velocity.
teacher.incline.step7.title: Knowledge Summary
teacher.incline.step7.desc: The key to incline problems is correct force decomposition. Apply Newton's 2nd law along the incline direction. Friction always opposes motion.
